newsitem.title: INDIA: India HLL denies insider trading charge.
newsitem.headline: India HLL denies insider trading charge.

text.p: Multinational firm Hindustan Lever Ltd (HLL) on Tuesday denied it had indulged in insider trading as alleged by the Securities and Exchange Board of India (SEBI).

"HLL clarifies that the purchase transactions by HLL and Mr. R. Gopalakrishnan were made in an open and transparent manner and after strictly observing self-discipline and professional ethics in dealing with Group companies' shares," the company said in a statement.
The company was responding to a "communication of findings" sent to the firm on Monday by the market regulator, in which SEBI demanded an explanation on certain transactions in shares by HLL.
"According to our findings the company had information which was not available to the general public when it bought shares," SEBI executive director L.K. Singhvi told Reuters.
HLL is the Indian subsidiary of Anglo-Dutch conglomerate Unilever Plc. HLL's shares rose 17.5 rupees to 1,533 rupees, on its 1997 first half results.

HLL said net profits for the first six months of the year had risen to 2.56 billion rupees from 1.85 billion in the year-ago period, but the earlier figure does not include the effects of affiliate Brooke Bond Lipton India's merger with it.
SEBI said it had found that HLL had bought 800,000 shares of Brooke Bond Lipton India Ltd about two weeks before it announced in April 1996 a merger of it with HLL.
"This amounted to a case of insider trading," he said.
On being told the company had denied the allegation, he said: "We haven't got a reply. We have given them two weeks' time. We'll wait for it."
HLL admitted that it had purchased 800,000 shares of Brooke Bond, but said it was not in possession of price-sensitive information.
"The deal was concluded much before the announcement of the merger and much before the company became aware of the recommended swap ratio in mid-April 1996," the HLL statement said.
It said Brooke Bond's then managing director R. Gopalakrishnan had bought 2,500 shares, but this was about eight months before a a decision on the merger was taken.
"Mr. Gopalakrishnan's decision to buy the shares ...after obtaining permission of the then Chairman was not influenced by any price-sensitive information ..." the statement added.
